compiler for real-time Arabic maqam accompaniment
with a streaming text-to-music model
Jiaxin Du<sup>a</sup>, Boulbaba Abdeljaouad<sup>a</sup>, Yong Zhuang<sup>a</sup>, Haoyu Li<sup>a</sup>
<sup>a</sup>Grand Valley State University, Allendale, MI, USA
Abstract
Arabic maqam music—microtonal, modal, and built on ornamented call-
and-response—is among the traditions most underserved by generative music
models, whose training frameworks remain predominantly Western and
equal-tempered. Real-time accompaniment sharpens this gap: an AI partner
must listen, adapt dynamically, and respect idiomatic microtonal structures.
Streaming text-to-music models provide strong generative capabilities but
lack precise control interfaces. We present MazzikaAI, a knowledge-based
system that uses natural language as the actuator of a real-time control loop.
By compiling live MIDI, gesture, and inferred harmony into continuously
updated text prompts, MazzikaAI steers an unmodified streaming generator
(Google Lyria RealTime) without requiring model fine-tuning. The system
embeds expert knowledge of six core maqamat, characteristic ornaments, and
ensemble dynamics, maintaining real-time responsiveness with sub-second
key-to-audible-update latency. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that
dynamic prompt compilation reliably grounds generation in microtonal scales,
significantly increasing of-grid quarter-tone content over baseline generation.
Beyond its core implementation, MazzikaAI illustrates how deterministic
knowledge-based rules can efectively bridge expert, non-Western musical
traditions and un-fine-tuned foundation models. This architecture establishes a
scalable paradigm for real-time human-AI co-creation, ofering a generalizable
blueprint for interactive accompaniment, adaptive music education, and
culturally inclusive generative audio across diverse global idioms.
Keywords: Expert system, Knowledge-based system, Prompt engineering,
Real-time music generation, Human–AI co-creation, Arabic maqam

1. Introduction
A good accompanist listens continuously, anticipates, and supports the
soloist without overtaking them. Reproducing that behaviour computationally
has motivated decades of work on interactive music systems, from rule-
and agent-based improvisers (Lewis, 2000; Rowe, 1993) to statistical style
companions (Pachet, 2003; Thom, 2000). Neural music models have transformed
the raw quality of what can be generated: text-conditioned systems synthesize
convincing full-band audio across a wide stylistic range (Agostinelli et al.,
2023; Copet et al., 2023; Evans et al., 2024). The property that makes
them powerful—end-to-end generation of audio from a coarse conditioning
signal—also makes them hard to steer at the temporal grain a live performance
demands. A model that renders a beautiful minute of music from one prompt
is not, by itself, a bandmate that reacts to the note just played.
Streaming, prompt-steerable models such as Lyria RealTime (Google Deep-
Mind, 2025) and Magenta RealTime (Lyria Team, Google DeepMind, 2025)
narrow the gap: they emit audio incrementally and accept prompt updates
mid-session. But they supply a control surface without a control policy. They
answer “given this prompt now, what audio streams out?” and leave open the
question a live accompaniment system must answer: how should that prompt be
produced and continuously revised from what a human is playing at this instant?
Driven by a static prompt, a streaming model produces a generic backing track
that ignores the soloist. Symbolic and score-conditioned models (Huang et al.,
2019; Roberts et al., 2018; Hadjeres et al., 2017) ofer fine control but forgo
the timbral realism of audio models, and adapting either family to a new idiom

vals, characteristic ornaments, and modal resting tones, is poorly represented
in both the training distributions and the control vocabularies of mainstream
models (Shahriar and Tariq, 2021; Bozkurt et al., 2014).

held—into precise, musically-literate prose, a general streaming model becomes

MazzikaAI realizes this as a deployed system (Fig. 1). A human plays a MIDI
keyboard in the browser; a React front end captures note events, sustain, hand
gestures, and voice commands and streams them over a WebSocket to a Python
backend. The backend maintains a rolling estimate of the performance—density,
register, motion, dynamic arc, phrase boundaries, inferred harmony—and, on
each meaningful change, compiles that state into a prompt streamed to a text-to-
music model (i.e. Lyria RealTime). Two generative streams run concurrently:
a melodic ensemble that follows and answers the soloist, and a tempo-locked
percussion bed. Returned audio is decoded and scheduled for low-latency play-
back beneath the player’s own piano. The system is designed around vintage
Arabic maqam performance—its deepest knowledge, bespoke controller, and all
output-quality experiments target that idiom—and drives the model entirely
through prompt design; the same compiler retargets to eight further Western
genres by authoring new prompt fragments alone (Appendix Appendix A).

2. Related Work and Positioning
Table 1 places MazzikaAI against the five families of prior work it draws on,
along the axes that matter for live accompaniment: what the system is steered
through, at what granularity, what it costs to adapt to a new idiom, whether
it generates streaming audio, and whether it supports microtonal non-Western
modes.
Knowledge-based systems for music. Encoding musical expertise as an explicit
rule base is among the oldest ambitions of intelligent systems. Ebcioğlu’s
CHORAL (Ebcioğlu, 1988) harmonized Bach chorales with hundreds of hand-
authored rules; Cope’s EMI (Cope, 1992) recombined corpus signatures un-
der rule-based control; Rowe (Rowe, 1993) organized machine musicianship as
listening, interpretation, and rule-governed response. MazzikaAI deliberately
retains the two properties these share—the knowledge is inspectable and the
inference is deterministic—and replaces only what historically bounded them,
the symbolic efector, with a pretrained streaming generator addressed in prose,
in the spirit of recent eforts to unify foundation models with explicit knowledge
representations (Pan et al., 2024).
Interactive and co-creative systems. Voyager (Lewis, 2000) negotiated musical
agency alongside a human; the Continuator (Pachet, 2003) learned a player’s
style online and extended their phrases; BoB (Thom, 2000) traded solos
with a musician; and ReaLJam (Scarlatos et al., 2025) recently demonstrated
live human–AI jamming with a reinforcement-learning-tuned transformer.
The turn-taking dynamics these systems exploit are well documented
ethnomusicologically (Monson, 1996). MazzikaAI performs the same listen-
then-respond cycle, but couples the listening machinery to a large pretrained
audio model mediated by language rather than to a bespoke symbolic composer.

3. System Architecture
MazzikaAI is a three-tier system—browser client, Python backend, cloud
generative model—connected by a single bidirectional WebSocket (Fig. 1). Four
design commitments shape it. (i) Text is the sole point of control: the generator
is a black box that consumes prose and emits audio, so the deployed model can be
replaced without touching the control layer. (ii) Idiom is injected, not learned:
every prompt carries explicit grounding for the active mode, including negative
guidance against Western tonality. (iii) The performer conducts: rather than
a fixed band, the player toggles ensemble sections in and out and the compiler
actively suppresses the rest. (iv) Re-steering is gated: a coarse control signa-
ture decides when the live stream may be re-prompted, trading responsiveness
against stability.
Client and transport. A React/TypeScript application captures four input
modalities: note events (note_on/note_off, velocity, CC64 sustain) through
the Web MIDI API (W3C, 2015); hand gestures recognized on-device with
MediaPipe Hands (Lugaresi et al., 2019); spoken commands through the Web
Speech API; and a Learn Mode that parses MusicXML in-browser and delegates
scanned PDF pages to Gemini optical music recognition. The performer’s own
notes are rendered locally by a sampled grand piano, so the human’s sound is
never delayed by the network round trip. Every input becomes a small JSON
message: midi_event, control_update (genre, maqam, tempo; debounced
to ∼400 ms), gesture, section_toggle, and a tick heartbeat every 250 ms
that advances time-dependent state when no notes arrive. The backend replies
with state_update messages (estimated state and compiled prompt) and
audio_chunk messages tagged source∈{melody,percussion}.

generative model—connected by a single bidirectional WebSocket (Fig. 1). Four
design commitments shape it. (i) Text is the sole point of control: the generator
is a black box that consumes prose and emits audio, so the deployed model can be
replaced without touching the control layer. (ii) Idiom is injected, not learned:
every prompt carries explicit grounding for the active mode, including negative
guidance against Western tonality. (iii) The performer conducts: rather than
a fixed band, the player toggles ensemble sections in and out and the compiler
actively suppresses the rest. (iv) Re-steering is gated: a coarse control signa-
ture decides when the live stream may be re-prompted, trading responsiveness
against stability.
Client and transport. A React/TypeScript application captures four input
modalities: note events (note_on/note_off, velocity, CC64 sustain) through
the Web MIDI API (W3C, 2015); hand gestures recognized on-device with
MediaPipe Hands (Lugaresi et al., 2019); spoken commands through the Web
Speech API; and a Learn Mode that parses MusicXML in-browser and delegates
scanned PDF pages to Gemini optical music recognition. The performer’s own
notes are rendered locally by a sampled grand piano, so the human’s sound is
never delayed by the network round trip. Every input becomes a small JSON
message: midi_event, control_update (genre, maqam, tempo; debounced
to ∼400 ms), gesture, section_toggle, and a tick heartbeat every 250 ms
that advances time-dependent state when no notes arrive. The backend replies
with state_update messages (estimated state and compiled prompt) and
audio_chunk messages tagged source∈{melody,percussion}.

3.2. Why Two Decoupled Streams
MazzikaAI runs two independent Lyria sessions because melodic accom-
paniment and rhythmic bed obey diferent clocks. The melodic engine has
mute_drums enabled and no fixed BPM lock; it is re-prompted as harmony,
register and phrasing evolve. The percussion engine, once triggered by gesture,
runs continuously as a tempo-locked 4/4 bed at the selected BPM, independent
of the soloist, cycling through escalating style patterns and using tighter gen-
eration parameters to stay literal and sparse. Their control signals genuinely
conflict: the melodic voice must be free to breathe, slow, or rest to follow the
performer, whereas a groove must remain metronomically steady, and folding
both into one prompt would force one to compromise the other. Separation also
isolates a hard model constraint—Lyria cannot change BPM on a live stream,
so a tempo change forces a full disconnect-and-reconnect, which the percussion
engine can absorb without interrupting the melodic conversation.

Everything the system knows about music is hand-authored prose and num-

5. Implementation
The client is a React 19/TypeScript single-page application bundled by Vite;
all audio, input and vision capabilities come from native browser APIs. The
backend is a FastAPI service served by Uvicorn, depending on google-genai for
both Lyria RealTime generation and Gemini vision (optical music recognition in
Learn Mode) and on NumPy and soundfile for audio packing. Every hot-path
message travels over a single persistent WebSocket, keeping per-event overhead
low and connection setup of the latency path.
Streaming engine. The generative model is encapsulated in an asyn-
chronous LyriaEngine wrapping one live music session against the
models/lyria-realtime-exp endpoint. It exposes a small idempotent
surface: update_controls() pushes a weighted prompt [(text, 1.0)] and a
generation config, and caches both so each is re-sent only when it actually
changes; play() and stop() gate the stream. A background receive loop packs
each incoming 48 kHz stereo PCM chunk into a WAV container, base64-encodes
it, and enqueues it on a bounded queue, dropping the oldest chunk when
full—trading a dropped frame under load for a hard cap on end-to-end latency.
Stopping an engine drains the queue so stale audio never plays after the band
has been silenced. The engine treats a normally-completed receive stream
and a ConnectionClosed/APIError identically, clearing the session handle so
the next control tick reconnects transparently; transient drops and server-side
stream expiry are therefore invisible to the performer.
Two-engine orchestration. On every inbound message—and on each 250 ms
tick—the backend loop recomputes the shared state and then advances each
engine under its own gating logic. The melodic engine sounds only once at least
one section is conducted in and the warmup gate has passed; it stays active
while the soloist plays or within four seconds of the last note, after which it
stops and resets its control signature so a fresh prompt is issued on return.
The percussion engine is armed by a flag raised by gesture or voice and then
plays continuously until stopped; its signature is simply (bpm, style index). A
BPM change on either engine forces a disconnect-and-reconnect, and a session
detected as “triggered but not playing” is reset and restarted.

Multimodal control. Four modalities funnel into the same session state. MIDI:
note-on, note-of and CC64 sustain are decoded per input device and forwarded
with note, velocity, event type and timestamp. Gesture: a MediaPipe
Hands (Lugaresi et al., 2019) pipeline (maxNumHands= 2, confidence 0.7) infers

poses—index-only toggles percussion, open palm toggles the ensemble. Each
must be held for 700 ms before acting, followed by a 2–3 s cooldown, with hold

gated by confidence
and at most eight words, parsed against a rule set
requiring an explicit action word paired with a target; a 1.5 s deduplication
window prevents double firing. Learn Mode: MusicXML and .mxl are parsed
entirely in-browser; PDF scores are rendered to page images with PDF.js and
sent to Gemini vision, which returns a structured note list, with model fallbacks
tried newest-first.
Constraints that shaped the design. Four properties of the deployed generator
determined non-obvious choices. Lyria cannot change tempo on an open stream,
so BPM changes are implemented as reconnects and the percussion bed is
tempo-locked by design. The API exposes no stem-level mixing, so instrument
control is prompt-level and best-efort. Re-prompting on every note caused
audible thrashing, motivating the fingerprint-based gate. And the model has
no notion of the human’s own sound, so keeping the AI behind the soloist is
done with client-side attenuation plus explicit space-enforcing clauses in the
prompt. The recurring theme is that fine-grained control over a general model
is obtained without touching weights: the levers are prompt design, generation-
config scheduling, connection-lifecycle management, and client-side mixing.

maqam.

The most consistent feedback concerned temporal responsiveness. The per-
formers perceived the accompaniment as holding an essentially constant tempo
rather than breathing with their playing—the ensemble kept its own clock. This
observation is consistent with the system’s construction. The generator’s tempo
is fixed for the lifetime of a stream; the percussion bed is tempo-locked by
design; and the melodic engine’s “following” is semantic rather than metric—the
compiler tracks register, density, dynamics, harmony, and phrase boundaries,
but performs no beat tracking on the performer’s onsets, so nothing in the
control loop re-anchors generation to the actual pulse. The compiler currently
controls what the accompaniment plays more precisely than when.
This finding has three consequences. It identifies tempo and timing fit as
a rated construct—distinct from the reaction-latency sense of responsiveness

argument: turn-taking headroom absorbs reaction delay but does not substitute
for beat-level entrainment. And it places beat tracking with tempo re-anchoring
at musically safe boundaries at the head of the future-work agenda.
